headline: Tenki yohō is 天気 (tenki, “weather”) plus 予報 (yohō, “forecast”).
Tsunagu is a verbalization of 綱 (tsuna, “rope”).
Daijin is from Middle Chinese 大臣 (MC dajH dzyin).
Saru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sar-.
Haba resembles Greater Central Philippine *habaʔ (“long (object)”), but the page says that is likely coincidental.
Shōnin is 承 (shō, “agree to”) plus 認 (nin, “recognize”).
Tani, “valley”, is simply listed as from Old Japanese.
Hoho went from popo to fofo to hoho, and appears in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938 CE.
Risō may be a Japanese coinage from 理 (ri, “reason, principle”) plus 想 (sō, “thought, thinking”), first cited in an 1877 translation of Mill's Utilitarianism.
Henji is a Sinicization of 返り事 (kaerigoto), from Old Japanese kaferigoto, “reply, response”.
Mizuumi, “lake”, is 水 (mizu, “water”) plus 海 (umi, “sea”).
Shokubutsu is from Middle Chinese 植物 (MC dzyik mjut).
Yōroppa is from Portuguese Europa; some sources say Dutch, but Dutch phonology makes that less likely.
Sorezore is a reduplication of それ (sore, “that”), with sore voiced to zore by rendaku.
Sei, “surname”, is from Middle Chinese 姓, the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
Sakai, “border”, is the stem of the obsolete verb 境う (sakau, “to divide, to form a boundary between things”).
Atatameru is the root of 暖か (atataka, “warm”) plus -meru, “-en, -ify”.
Daishō is 大 (dai, “big, large”) plus 小 (shō, “small, little”): size as “big-small”.
Kanjō is probably a Middle Chinese compound, literally “investigate + to make something settled”.
The abacus reached Japan from China in the Muromachi period (1336–1573), and soroban is first attested in a 1595 trilingual dictionary.
Yo was spelled with the phonetic 用 in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and has since taken on a more literary sense.
Sugi's kanji 杉 is an ateji (当て字), and the word is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Shima, “island”, is possibly related to Baekje 斯麻 (*syema, “island”) and Middle Korean 셤 (syem).
Semeru is from the classical lower bigrade verb せむ, cognate with 攻める (semeru) and 狭い (semai).
Jama was originally a Buddhist term, from Middle Chinese 邪魔, literally “wrong, evil, perverse” plus “devil, demon”.
Yurui appears to be derived from the archaic verb 揺る (yuru, “to shake, sway”).
Shodō is 書 (sho, “writing”) plus 道 (-dō, “-manship”).
Sofu is from Middle Chinese 祖父, the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
Chiji shortens 知某州事, “one who knows matters concerning the county/province”.
Nanboku is Middle Chinese 南北, literally “south and north”.
